title: Mystery plays
hookLine: townspeople acted the Bible on wagons: the shipwrights built Noah's ark

lines: A WAGON ROLLS INTO THE STREET.
THE NEXT STORY ROLLS UP BEHIND.
cards: A summer morning in an English town, and a wooden wagon creaks around the corner. On it, a man with a hammer is building a boat.
He's playing Noah, and the men helping him build real boats all week: they're the town's shipwrights. The wagon moves on to the next corner, and another rolls up behind it with the next story.
On one of them, later, the crowd laughs when Noah's wife refuses to get on board. All day long, the whole Bible comes down the street.

teach.h: CREATION TO JUDGMENT, ON THE STREET.
teach.b: Mystery plays were cycles of short Bible plays, put on by ordinary townspeople in English towns like York and Chester.
They usually ran from creation to the last judgment: the fall, Noah, Abraham and Isaac, the shepherds at Bethlehem, the crucifixion, the empty tomb.
Each play was given to a trade guild, and the guilds often got the scene that fit their work. In York, the shipwrights staged the building of the ark.

In Genesis, God tells Noah, in the King James Bible, "Make thee an ark of gopher wood." And then, "Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he." Who better to swing those hammers?
Each play went up on a pageant wagon, a stage on wheels, and the wagons stopped at set places so different crowds could see each scene in turn.
The plays were in English, the language people spoke at home, at a time when church services were in Latin. They mixed holy and ordinary. Shepherds grumble about the cold before the angel comes.
Noah's wife, in some plays, would rather stay with her friends than climb into the ark. People laughed, and then they watched a carpenter's son die on a cross.
A town that acted these stories year after year carried them in its body: the lines, the hammers, the costumes kept in a guild's chest. Scripture wasn't only read to them. It was something they did.

how: Some English towns, including York and Chester, still stage their mystery plays, sometimes on wagons in the streets, and some churches put on nativity plays with children at Christmas.

games.q: you're planning your town's Bible plays. the building of Noah's ark needs a cast. who gets the scene?
games.why: in York, the shipwrights staged the building of the ark. the guilds often got the scene that fit their work.

practice: Pick one Bible story you know well, Noah and the ark, the lost sheep, the Good Samaritan, and cast it in your head: who plays the boat-builder, who gets to be the stubborn one, and what would you use for props, a broom, a blanket, a cardboard box?
If there's a child in your life, picture acting it out together; if not, walk through the scene yourself, just to see it from the inside. If you pray, you can give thanks for the story.
